verdicts.strongest_argument: Every constituent fact here is wire copy, and the two ABM-side facts are ABM's own published words with a stated cause that is not airline distress. The airline cuts: American's first 2026 guidance cut was 2026-04-23 and Alaska's suspension was April 2026 -- both BEFORE ABM guided on 2026-06-05, so the claim's framing ('after ABM last guided') is factually wrong for two of its three carriers. The claim's own source also reports Delta affirming $6.50-7.50 and United RAISING to $9-11, so the sector bifurcated rather than broke, and Delta/United are the carriers most relevant to major-hub turn volume. American's six route suspensions were announced 2026-06-04 and run 2026-08-05 to 2026-10-05 -- entirely outside ABM's fiscal Q3, which ended 31 July; they land in Q4. On the ABM side, the 5.25% Aviation margin is arithmetically correct ($16.3M/$310.8M) but was disclosed by ABM itself on 2026-06-05 and attributed by management to 'weather-related and ramp-up cost inefficiencies' (the London Heathrow ramp), alongside 20% Aviation revenue growth on 'healthy domestic air travel trends' -- and the stock rose 6.67% that day with all of it on the table. The bridge is the weak part: ABM bills per turn, per cabin, per parking transaction and per shuttle hour against traffic and airport/airline contracts, not against airline EPS; a fuel-driven EPS collapse at a carrier whose revenue is still growing does not reduce ABM's billable units inside a 92-day window. The one channel that genuinely lands in 1 May - 31 July is ABM's own diesel/gasoline bill on its bus fleet, and ABM's own marketing puts that fleet at '800+ buses' rather than 1,000+; on plausible utilisation a $1/gal move is order $2M pre-tax a quarter, roughly $0.02-0.03 of EPS against a $0.97 consensus -- under 1% of the quarter and an order of magnitude inside the 3.33% deadband. Verdict: I concede the facts about the airlines and about ABM's Q2 margin, and reject the bridge -- this is true about the source companies and close to worthless about ABM's Q3 P&L.

prior_publication.what_it_says: ABM's own Q2 FY26 release: Aviation revenue $310.8M and operating profit $16.3M vs $260.1M and $16.5M, margin pressure attributed by management to weather-related and ramp-up cost inefficiencies, with FY26 adjusted EPS reaffirmed at $3.85-$4.15.
American cut its 2026 profit guidance on high jet fuel prices in April 2026 -- six weeks before ABM guided on 2026-06-05, not after it.
The claim's own source: it dates Alaska's guidance suspension to April 2026, and reports Delta affirming FY26 at $6.50-$7.50 and United raising FY26 to $9-$11 in the same cycle.
American's six fuel-driven route suspensions were announced 2026-06-04 and are effective 2026-08-05 to 2026-10-05, i.e. after ABM's fiscal Q3 closed on 31 July.

ABM's own aviation fast-facts page puts the airport bus fleet at '800+ buses' and aircraft cleaning at ~1.3 million aircraft a year, which caps the fuel-exposure arithmetic below the claim's 1,000+ figure.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The strongest single piece of baseline evidence runs against this claim: ABM printed +6.67% on 2026-06-05, the day the 5.25% Aviation margin and the fixed-cost ramp drag were both disclosed, and it went on to set its 52-week high of $50.12 in late July (spot 47.02 is only 4.74% below it) with the July airline cuts already on the wire. The 20-day run-up of -3.13% on 15.2% annualised vol is noise, not bracing. The options chain is unusable (188% ATM spread on 93 contracts of open interest), so there is no put bid to point to in either direction. Nothing in the tape says the market is positioned for an aviation shortfall, but nothing says it has ignored one either -- and the drift from ~50 to 47 over August is at least directionally consistent with mild de-rating.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that a named ABM aviation customer cut scheduled block hours or ground-handling scope inside 1 May - 31 July 2026, or an ABM disclosure showing fuel is not passed through on the shuttle contracts, at a scale above roughly $10M of quarterly revenue.

verdicts.strongest_argument: The FIX and EMCOR facts check out exactly as stated -- FIX revenue $3.27bn (+50%), EPS $12.53 vs $6.53, backlog $14.06bn at 30 June vs $8.12bn; EMCOR to $20.0-20.5bn from $18.5-19.25bn and $32.00-33.25 from $28.25-29.75 -- but both are the loudest wire-copy events of the July reporting season, EMCOR traded up 7.1% on its raise, and the AI/data-centre capex cycle is the single most-told story in this market. Two things break the claim as stated. First, the premise 'in a stock that has not participated at all' is false on the tape: ABM was $49.36 on 2026-07-30, up 23.7% over the prior 90 days, and set its 52-week high at $50.12 in that same window -- spot 47.02 is 4.7% below it and 25.8% above the low. ABM participated; it has since given back ~5%, which is a different and much smaller claim. Second, the ramp is not just published, it is in the consensus number: ABM guided the back half on 2026-06-05 to 'meaningfully higher volume in ATS and M&D' with improved mix, explicitly citing 'battery energy storage systems and datacenter-related services' behind ATS's 27% growth, reaffirmed FY26 at $3.85-4.15, and the sell side now carries Q3 FY26 at $0.97 against $0.82 actual a year ago -- an 18% step-up already required of the print. The bridge is also thinner than the size of the FIX/EME numbers suggests: FIX and EME are pure-play hyperscale MEP construction; ABM's Technical Solutions is $267.3M of revenue at a 6.3% operating margin, about 11-12% of ABM, doing retrofit, microgrid, BESS, EV charging and mission-critical facility services. A +50% quarter at FIX says the cycle is alive; it says nothing about ABM's own project timing, which is precisely the variable that produced -9.07% on 2025-06-06 and -8.67% on 2025-03-12. Even a strong ATS quarter -- say 35% growth with 100bp of mix -- is order $5-8M of incremental operating profit, roughly $0.06-0.10 of EPS, and much of that is the guided path rather than a surprise. What keeps this off 90 is one genuinely under-drawn item: nobody has modelled an inflection in ABM's own ATS backlog disclosure on the scale of FIX's +73% or EMCOR's +44% RPO, and that number does land in this print.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Comfort Systems' record Q2 2026 -- revenue $3.27bn up 50%, EPS $12.53, backlog $14.06bn up 73% -- was fully reported the day it printed.
EMCOR raised FY26 revenue to $20.0-20.5bn from $18.5-19.25bn and EPS to $32.00-33.25 from $28.25-29.75, with record RPOs of $17.14bn.
EMCOR traded up 7.1% on the raise -- the read-through was priced into the source name the same day.

ABM itself guided the back half to 'meaningfully higher volume in ATS and M&D' with improved mix, and named battery energy storage and datacenter-related services as the drivers of ATS's 27% growth to $267.3M revenue / $16.8M operating profit.
Consensus for the 2026-09-08 print is $0.97 of EPS against $0.82 a year earlier, so the guided back-half step-up is already the number ABM has to clear.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The tape refutes the claim's own premise. ABM's 52-week high of $50.12 was set in late July 2026, the exact fortnight of the FIX (07-23) and EMCOR (07-30) prints, with ABM at $49.36 on 07-30 and up 23.7% over 90 days; spot 47.02 is 4.74% below that high and 25.76% above the low. That is participation followed by a 5% giveback, not non-participation. The +6.67% reaction on 2026-06-05 is the market already paying for the ATS ramp story on the day ABM told it. With the chain unusable (188% ATM spread, 93 contracts) there is no skew to argue that upside is being sold cheaply.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: An ABM-specific datapoint -- a named hyperscale or utility-scale ATS award, a disclosed ATS backlog figure, or an intra-quarter ABM comment -- showing ATS running materially above the guided ramp rather than in line with it, plus evidence that Q3 consensus of $0.97 has not already absorbed it.

interactions: The two findings rest on the same ABM-side document and read it in opposite directions. ABM's 2026-06-05 Q2 FY26 release simultaneously contains the Aviation margin compression that ABM#0 treats as deterioration (revenue $310.8M, operating profit $16.3M, 5.25% vs 6.34%) and the Technical Solutions strength and back-half ramp language that ABM#1 treats as acceleration (revenue $267.3M, operating profit $16.8M, +27%, 'meaningfully higher volume in ATS and M&D'). Both are true at once, and the market has already netted them: the stock rose 6.67% on the day both were published, then ran to a 52-week high of $50.12 in late July. Scoring them as two independent surprises double-counts one already-priced disclosure, and because they carry opposite signs and near-identical priced-in weight they should very largely cancel in this name's score rather than adding. A second, smaller overlap: both claims share the source date 2026-07-23 and both depend on the same July-reporting-season news cycle, which is the most heavily covered two weeks of the quarter -- neither can claim obscurity of publication. Note also that ABM#0's timing premise is internally contradicted by its own cited article, which dates Alaska's suspension to April 2026 and shows Delta affirming and United raising.
